public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1065

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/1065](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1065)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos1065

/--
Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p = 2^k * q + 1$
for some prime $q$ and $k ≥ 0$?

This is mentioned as B46
in [Unsolved Problems in Number Theory](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-0-387-26677-0)
by *Richard K. Guy*
 -/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1065.parts.i :
    answer(sorry) ↔ Set.Infinite {p | ∃ q k, p.Prime ∧ q.Prime ∧ p = 2^k * q + 1} := by
  sorry

/--
Are there infinitely many primes $p$ such that $p = 2^k 3^l q + 1$
for some prime $q$ and $k ≥ 0$, $l ≥ 0$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_1065.parts.ii : answer(sorry) ↔
    Set.Infinite {p | ∃ q k l, p.Prime ∧ q.Prime ∧ p = 2^k * 3^l * q + 1} := by
  sorry

end Erdos1065

reformulations.difference: The docstring cites Guy's B46. Guy's wording, as the OEIS entries A074781 and A339465 paraphrase it (both citing UPINT 3rd ed., B46, p. 154), asks for infinitely many primes p with (p-1)/P(p-1) = 2^k, where P is the greatest prime factor. The Lean follows erdosproblems.com instead: p = 2^k*q + 1 for some prime q and k : ℕ, with no requirement that q be the greatest prime factor of p-1.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: If p - 1 = 2^k q with q prime, every prime divisor of p-1 is 2 or q, and 2 ≤ q, so q = P(p-1) and (p-1)/P(p-1) = 2^k. Conversely, if (p-1)/P(p-1) = 2^k, take q = P(p-1). So the two sets agree for p ≥ 3. At p = 2 they can differ only by the one element 2 (under the OEIS convention gpf(1) = 1), which cannot change `Set.Infinite`. Proved in Lean as `ReviewEquiv.guyI_eq` in /workspace/review/equiv.lean (axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound). Numerically, the Lean set equals OEIS A074781 for every p < 888.

reformulations.difference: Guy's wording (via the OEIS A339465 comment) asks for (p-1)/P(p-1) = 2^k 3^l. The Lean follows erdosproblems.com: p = 2^k*3^l*q + 1 for some prime q and k, l : ℕ. Here q need not be the greatest prime factor of p-1; for example q = 2 with l ≥ 1. Note also that the OEIS sequence A339465 itself restricts to exponents ≥ 1 only to stay disjoint from A074781.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every prime divisor of 2^k 3^l q is 2, 3 or q. If q ≥ 3, then q = P(p-1). If q = 2 and l = 0, then P(p-1) = 2. If q = 2 and l ≥ 1, rewrite p-1 = 2^(k+1) 3^(l-1) * 3, so P(p-1) = 3. In every case (p-1)/P(p-1) is 3-smooth. The converse direction is immediate. The sets agree for p ≥ 3, and p = 2 cannot change `Set.Infinite`. Proved in Lean as `ReviewEquiv.guyII_eq` in /workspace/review/equiv.lean. Numerically, the Lean set equals A074781 ∪ A339465 for every p < 888.

review.notes:
Both declarations transcribe the erdosproblems.com statement directly. The p, q, k, l binders elaborate to ℕ (checked with #print), and the precedence is 2^k * q + 1 = (2^k)*q + 1, as intended. In each part the right-hand side of `answer(sorry)` has the same polarity as the source's question ("Are there infinitely many…?" ↔ `Set.Infinite`).

Part (ii) reads l ≥ 0. That is the natural reading of the source's follow-up "Or p = 2^k 3^l q + 1?" after "k ≥ 0", and it makes (ii) a weakening of (i). A reading with l ≥ 1 is not supported by the source; the OEIS A339465 restriction to exponents ≥ 1 exists only to keep that sequence disjoint from A074781.

Neither part is trivially settled. Part (i) contains the safe/Sophie Germain primes (k = 1) and the Fermat primes (q = 2). Part (ii) contains all Pierpont primes other than 2, and the repository itself tags their infinitude `research open` (Wikipedia/PierpontPrime.lean).

Status: erdosproblems.com (accessed 2026-09-23) shows OPEN with 0 proof claims, and the teorth database also records open. This matches `@[category research open]` on both parts, so there are no status issues.

I could not read Guy's B46 text directly (Springer paywall; archive.org lending copy restricted). Its content was checked through the OEIS entries' paraphrase and citation, and the gpf formulation was proved equivalent in Lean.
